arguments.claim: AQAADI would not close the door to the possibility that the RPD may, in some cases, have a meaningful advantage, and stresses that the meaningful advantage inquiry must be properly undertaken in every case.

arguments.quote: The Minister counters that, while demeanour evidence has its shortcomings, its use remains permissible under Canadian law (see R v RD, 2016 ONCA 574 at para 25). The Minister argues that fact-finding is not a science but rather a difficult and complex process to which demeanour has some relevance, referring to the following extract from R v NS:
arguments.claim: While demeanour evidence has shortcomings, its use remains permissible under Canadian law, and fact-finding is a difficult and complex process to which demeanour has some relevance.
arguments.outcome_note: Demeanour evidence is permissible but must be properly analyzed for meaningful advantage.

arguments.quote: I have been urged by the interveners to distinguish this body of case law, owing to the unique context of refugee determinations. I am indeed mindful of studies and literature that give pause about, as well as rationale to rethink, the basis of credibility determinations, including the work of Professor Hilary Cameron-Evans in her recently published book Refugee Law’s Fact-Finding Crisis: Truth, Risk and Wrong Mistake, (Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2018).
arguments.claim: The interveners urge to distinguish the case law on demeanour evidence due to the unique context of refugee determinations, noting studies and literature that question credibility determinations.

arguments.quote: The RAD majority clearly had concerns about its inability to truly review, on a correctness standard, findings based on the RPD’s proximity to a witness, and elements that could not be translated into the record.
arguments.claim: The RAD majority had concerns about its inability to truly review, on a correctness standard, findings based on the RPD’s proximity to a witness and elements that could not be translated into the record.

arguments.quote: The RAD majority erred in failing to outline for future panels when the RPD’s general fact-finding advantage becomes a specific, meaningful advantage, which in turn would justify the application of a deferential standard of review.
arguments.claim: The RAD majority failed to outline when the RPD's general fact-finding advantage becomes a specific, meaningful advantage justifying a deferential standard of review.

arguments.quote: For instance, the Applicants have argued that IRPA integrates institutional deference, because a claimant cannot appeal to the RAD if the RPD finds their claim to be manifestly unfounded (IRPA, s 107.1) or to have no credible basis (IRPA, section 107(2)).
arguments.claim: IRPA integrates institutional deference because a claimant cannot appeal to the RAD if the RPD finds their claim manifestly unfounded or without credible basis.

arguments.quote: CARL/CCR, on the other hand, have focused on the idea of remedial deference. Remedial deference occurs when the RAD remits a matter to the RPD instead of substituting its own determination of the outcome of the refugee claim.
arguments.claim: CARL/CCR focus on remedial deference, where the RAD remits a matter to the RPD instead of substituting its own determination.

arguments.quote: In its analysis, the RAD was confronted with case law taking different positions on this issue. For instance, the RAD majority referred to cases pre-dating Huruglica, where the Federal Court found that it was an error for the RAD to use a reasonableness standard when reviewing the RPD’s credibility findings (see, for instance, Khachatourian v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 182 at paras 30–31). But the RAD also referred to decisions of this Court post-dating Huruglica, which held that the RAD should use a reasonableness standard in such circumstances (Al Moussawi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 441 at para 16; Sinnaraja v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 778 at para 23).
arguments.claim: The RAD majority referred to conflicting case law on whether a reasonableness standard should be used when reviewing RPD credibility findings.

arguments.quote: The RAD majority concluded that the level of deference to be shown to the RPD’s credibility findings was not the same as that owed on judicial review because, even where deference was warranted, the RAD still had to independently review the evidence on which the finding was based. In other words, the RAD majority held that a reasonableness type of review was appropriate so long as the RAD also engaged in an independent analysis of the evidence.
arguments.claim: The RAD majority concluded that the level of deference to RPD credibility findings is not the same as on judicial review because the RAD must independently review the evidence.

arguments.quote: Specifically, the RAD majority settled on a standard of RAD reasonableness, where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in making a credibility finding. The RAD majority said that, although RAD reasonableness was not the same as the judicial review reasonableness standard, it would still rely on the jurisprudence explaining and defining reasonableness in the context of judicial review.
arguments.claim: The RAD majority adopted a standard of RAD reasonableness where the RPD has a meaningful advantage in making credibility findings, relying on judicial review reasonableness jurisprudence.

arguments.quote: The RAD majority turned to Dunsmuir in concluding that it should assess both process and outcome. That is to say, the RPD’s finding would stand if it was the result of a comprehensible reasoning process, meaning that the RAD could read the RPD’s conclusion and understand how it was reached, and its outcome was supported by the evidence.
arguments.claim: The RAD majority applied Dunsmuir to assess both process and outcome, requiring the RPD's finding to be comprehensible and supported by evidence.

arguments.quote: The RAD majority’s view made it implicit that a reasonableness type of standard of review could be used if the RAD also conducted an independent assessment of the matter before it.
arguments.claim: The RAD majority implicitly held that a reasonableness standard could be used if the RAD also conducted an independent assessment.

arguments.quote: The Applicants argue that RAD reasonableness, the RAD’s concept of deference, is unreasonable because it results in a duplication of the Dunsmuir framework at the administrative level.
arguments.claim: The Applicants argue that RAD reasonableness is unreasonable because it duplicates the Dunsmuir framework at the administrative level.

arguments.quote: They say that this is contrary to Huruglica in which the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD is “not to review RPD decisions in the manner of a judicial review” (at para 37).
arguments.claim: The Applicants say RAD reasonableness is contrary to Huruglica, which held that the RAD is not to review RPD decisions like a judicial review.

arguments.quote: The Applicants argue that the RAD majority’s approach results in a situation of “double deference” as termed by Professor Daly in “Les appels administratifs au Canada” (2015) 93 Can Bar Rev 71 [Les appels] at 84. Double deference refers to the Federal Court being tasked with reviewing the reasonableness of the RAD’s own reasonableness analysis.
arguments.claim: The RAD majority's approach results in a situation of 'double deference', where the Federal Court reviews the reasonableness of the RAD's own reasonableness analysis.

arguments.quote: Accordingly, the Applicants argue that any expression of deference by the RAD should be less than in a reasonableness review and should not use the language of judicial review. They submit that no other result can be supported by the statutory scheme as set out by IRPA.
arguments.claim: Any expression of deference by the RAD should be less than in a reasonableness review and should not use the language of judicial review, as supported by the statutory scheme in IRPA.

arguments.quote: The Applicants also rely on Professor Daly’s analysis that the RAD is not a typical, generalist appeal tribunal, lacking the specialized expertise of the lower tribunal, but is rather a highly specialized tribunal itself (Les appels at 75–76).
arguments.claim: The RAD is a highly specialized tribunal itself, not a typical generalist appeal tribunal lacking the specialized expertise of the lower tribunal.

arguments.quote: The Minister argues that RAD reasonableness is sufficiently distinct from judicial review because the RAD must begin with an overall, independent assessment of the matter before it, while judicial review focuses on the decision‑maker’s reasons.
arguments.claim: RAD reasonableness is distinct from judicial review because the RAD must begin with an overall, independent assessment of the matter, while judicial review focuses on the decision-maker's reasons.

arguments.quote: RAD reasonableness, according to the Minister, is simply a term used by the RAD, with built-in flexibility that is both appropriate to the level of deference that the RAD should give to the RPD, and is thus reasonable.
arguments.claim: RAD reasonableness is a term used by the RAD with built-in flexibility appropriate to the level of deference the RAD should give to the RPD, and is thus reasonable.

arguments.quote: CARL/CCR argue that the RAD cannot independently assess the basis for a particular finding, while simultaneously reviewing it on a deferential standard. In their view, this exposes a fundamental and irreconcilable tension between the idea of a deferential review standard and the RAD’s duty to conduct an independent assessment.
arguments.claim: The RAD cannot independently assess the basis for a finding while reviewing it on a deferential standard, creating a fundamental tension between deferential review and the RAD's duty to conduct an independent assessment.

arguments.quote: CARL/CCR say that this tension is also apparent in the reasoning of the RAD minority where the single member warned:
arguments.claim: This tension is apparent in the RAD minority's reasoning where the single member warned about the independent assessment obligation.

arguments.quote: The RAD’s obligation to undertake an independent assessment bears further comment. In Huruglica, the Federal Court of Appeal did not specifically use the language of independent assessment. Nevertheless, subsequent cases have held that Huruglica endorsed a thorough, comprehensive, and independent review by the RAD (see, for instance, Gabila v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 574 at para 20; Marin v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 847 at paras 32–33).
arguments.claim: The RAD is obligated to undertake an independent assessment, which has been endorsed as a thorough, comprehensive, and independent review by the RAD in subsequent cases following Huruglica.

arguments.quote: It would seem, then, that an independent assessment could be seen as being antithetical to reasonableness review, and thus synonymous with correctness review (see Taqadees v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1072 at para 10; Daniel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1049 at paras 11–12; Kayitankore v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1030 at para 23).
arguments.claim: An independent assessment could be seen as antithetical to reasonableness review and synonymous with correctness review.

arguments.quote: It is his position that there was no error in the RAD majority using the term reasonableness, as this is just a label that describes a level of deference and it can be used outside of the judicial review context.
arguments.claim: The Minister argues that there was no error in the RAD majority using the term reasonableness, as it is just a label describing a level of deference and can be used outside the judicial review context.

arguments.quote: The Minister also argues that the RAD majority used the term reasonableness flexibly to fit the RAD’s particular context.
arguments.claim: The Minister also argues that the RAD majority used the term reasonableness flexibly to fit the RAD’s particular context.

arguments.quote: Furthermore, the RAD majority acknowledged that it was adopting a judicial review standard for its own purposes when it wrote that it would “assess reasonableness in the context of its particular role while attempting to avoid the development of a new gradation of that standard” (RAD Decision at para 70).
arguments.claim: The RAD majority acknowledged adopting a judicial review standard for its own purposes, aiming to avoid developing a new gradation of that standard.

arguments.quote: The Minister argued that the RAD majority was not required to select a standard less deferential than that in Dunsmuir.
arguments.claim: The Minister argued that the RAD majority was not required to select a standard less deferential than that in Dunsmuir.

arguments.quote: Awareness of this point is reflected in the analysis of the RAD minority, which was hesitant to adopt any standard that curtailed the RAD’s error-correcting role.
arguments.claim: The RAD minority was hesitant to adopt any standard that curtailed the RAD’s error-correcting role.

arguments.quote: I agree with the Applicants that, called by another name or not, reasonableness review as developed for the judicial review has no application in the RAD context.
arguments.claim: The Applicants argue that reasonableness review as developed for judicial review has no application in the RAD context.

arguments.quote: I note that while the interveners had originally sought a right of appeal in respect of this judgment (see Rozas del Solar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 156 at para 31), they abandoned this request at the hearing of this application.
arguments.claim: The interveners had sought a right of appeal in respect of this judgment but abandoned this request at the hearing of this application.

holdings.quote: The Applicants are a Chilean family of refugee claimants whose claim was rejected by both the first and second level administrative tribunals.
holdings.statement: The Applicants are a Chilean family of refugee claimants whose claim was rejected by both the first and second level administrative tribunals.

holdings.quote: They have come to this Court seeking judicial review of the second tribunal decision [Decision], made by the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD].
holdings.statement: They have come to this Court seeking judicial review of the second tribunal decision made by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

holdings.quote: The outcome of this judicial review turns on important but highly technical questions involving the standard of review applied by the RAD to its assessment of credibility findings made by the lower tribunal, the Refugee Protection Division [RPD].
holdings.statement: The judicial review concerns the standard of review applied by the RAD to credibility findings made by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD).

holdings.quote: The family – a husband, wife and their two daughters – are citizens of Chile, where they claim that a loan shark is threatening to harm them over an unpaid, high-interest debt.
holdings.statement: The family consists of a husband, wife and two daughters, citizens of Chile, claiming threats from a loan shark over unpaid debt.

holdings.quote: This claim was determined not to be credible and, as a result, rejected first by the RPD, and then on appeal by the RAD.
holdings.statement: The RPD found the claim not credible and rejected it, and the RAD upheld that rejection on appeal.

holdings.quote: For those not familiar with the refugee determination process, both the RPD and the RAD are divisions of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada [IRB] — the largest independent administrative tribunal in Canada specialized in refugee adjudication.
holdings.statement: The RPD and RAD are divisions of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB), an independent administrative tribunal specialized in refugee adjudication.

holdings.quote: The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], provides the IRB with its statutory jurisdiction.
holdings.statement: The IRB's jurisdiction is provided by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

holdings.quote: At first instance, an RPD member heard the Applicants’ claim over two days, on December 8, 2015 and January 7, 2016. The tribunal dismissed the claim in written reasons dated February 19, 2016, finding that the husband’s and wife’s stories were not credible and that adequate state protection was available to them in Chile.
holdings.statement: The RPD heard the Applicants' claim over two days in December 2015 and January 2016, and dismissed it in written reasons dated February 19, 2016, finding the husband’s and wife’s stories not credible and that adequate state protection was available in Chile.

holdings.quote: The Applicants appealed to the RAD. In all preceding cases, RAD appeals, like RPD hearings, had been decided by a single panel member.
holdings.statement: The Applicants appealed to the RAD, which had previously decided appeals by a single panel member.

holdings.quote: However, on June 22, 2016, the IRB Chairperson ordered the Applicants’ appeal to be heard by a three-member panel under section 163 of IRPA for the first time since the RAD’s establishment in December 2012.
holdings.statement: On June 22, 2016, the IRB Chairperson ordered the Applicants’ appeal to be heard by a three-member panel under section 163 of IRPA, the first such panel since the RAD’s establishment in 2012.

holdings.quote: The reason why the IRB Chairperson ordered a three-member panel goes back to a claim involving a different family of refugee claimants, a case ultimately appealed in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93 [Huruglica]. In Huruglica, the Federal Court of Appeal held that, when considering the RPD’s factual and legal conclusions on appeal, the RAD must typically apply a correctness standard of review.
holdings.statement: The IRB Chairperson’s decision to convene a three-member panel was influenced by the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Huruglica, which held that the RAD must typically apply a correctness standard of review to RPD’s factual and legal conclusions on appeal.

holdings.quote: What the Federal Court of Appeal left open in Huruglica, however, was the question of how the RAD should show restraint or deference to some of the RPD’s conclusions on credibility where the RPD was better-positioned to make them.
holdings.statement: Huruglica left open how the RAD should show restraint or deference to some RPD credibility conclusions where the RPD was better positioned to make them.

holdings.quote: Therefore, the IRB Chairperson decided that this RAD appeal provided the factual backdrop for a three-member panel, which has a precedential effect for future RAD and RPD panels (IRPA, s 171(c)). This would allow the RAD to develop its own law in appeals on credibility findings, as Huruglica had urged.
holdings.statement: The IRB Chairperson decided that this RAD appeal would provide the factual backdrop for a three-member panel to develop law on credibility findings appeals, as urged by Huruglica.

holdings.quote: The Applicants have asked the Federal Court to judicially review the RAD’s Decision under section 72(1) of IRPA.
holdings.statement: The Federal Court applies judicial review to the Refugee Appeal Division's decision under section 72(1) of IRPA.

holdings.quote: A judicial review is not an appeal or a rehearing of the Applicants’ case (Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1077 at para 9). Instead, the Federal Court’s role on judicial review is far more limited and supervisory in nature, namely to ensure that the tribunal’s decision is consistent with the rule of law (Mission Institution v Khela, 2014 SCC 24 at para 37).
holdings.statement: Judicial review is not an appeal or rehearing but a supervisory role to ensure the tribunal's decision complies with the rule of law.

holdings.quote: In other words, the Court’s task on judicial review is not to retry cases. With respect to the Applicants, this means that my role is not to decide their refugee claims. Rather, it is to review whether the RAD’s Decision contains reviewable errors (Tsleil-Waututh Nation v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 FCA 128 at paras 78, 85).
holdings.statement: The Court's task on judicial review is to determine if the decision contains reviewable errors, not to retry the case.

holdings.quote: Should the Court find such errors, the appropriate remedy in such cases is, in general, to send the matter back for redetermination.
holdings.statement: If reviewable errors are found, the usual remedy is to send the matter back for redetermination.

holdings.quote: In any judicial review, the Court must first select what standard of review applies to the issues raised. This is because the standard of review is the lens through which the Court analyzes the decision‑maker’s conclusions to determine whether judicial intervention is warranted (see R v Skinner, 2016 NSCA 54 [Skinner] at para 17).
holdings.statement: The Court must select the applicable standard of review—correctness or reasonableness—before analyzing the decision-maker's conclusions.

holdings.quote: Today, there are only two such lenses: correctness and reasonableness (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 [Dunsmuir] at para 34). Sometimes, the decision‑maker must answer the question exactly as the reviewer deems correct, or hit the bull’s eye. Nothing less will do for a correctness review, as there is no margin for error (Skinner at para 22); for a reasonableness review, the outer rings will do.
holdings.statement: There are two standards of review: correctness, requiring the decision-maker to be exactly right, and reasonableness, allowing a range of acceptable outcomes.

holdings.quote: Simply put, when a correctness lens is used, the reviewer decides the question before it exactly as it thinks it should. If the reviewer’s conclusion ends up being different than the decision‑maker’s, the reviewer will substitute its own answer as the correct one (Dunsmuir at para 50).
holdings.statement: Under correctness review, the Court substitutes its own answer if it differs from the decision-maker's.

holdings.quote: For other types of questions, there is no one correct answer. This is where a reasonableness standard of review applies, and where there is typically a range of acceptable approaches to and outcomes for the legal questions raised. The decision‑maker will have a margin of appreciation, or a range of acceptable solutions (Dunsmuir at para 47). Even if the conclusion is not the reviewer’s preferred solution, the decision‑maker’s process and outcome just has to fall somewhere in that range of possible outcomes, although, sometimes there is only one possible outcome.
holdings.statement: Under reasonableness review, the decision-maker has a margin of appreciation and the decision must fall within a range of acceptable outcomes.

holdings.quote: Of the two standards that comprise judicial review today, it should not be surprising, then, that reasonableness is far more common than correctness. Indeed, the Supreme Court has recently indicated that, “[i]n most cases, a contextual assessment leads to the conclusion that the appropriate standard of review is reasonableness” (West Fraser Mills Ltd v British Columbia (Workers’ Compensation Appeal Tribunal), 2018 SCC 22 [West Fraser] at para 8).
holdings.statement: Reasonableness is the more common standard of review in judicial review cases.

holdings.quote: Reasonableness – in name at least – thus appears to have become the default standard, not only in West Fraser, but also in other recent Supreme Court decisions such as Groia v Law Society of Upper Canada, 2018 SCC 27 (at paras 45–47). Certainly, where the decision‑maker interprets the legislation that created the tribunal – its home statute – there is a strong presumption of reasonableness (CHRC at para 27). Here, the RAD was interpreting various sections of IRPA, its home statute.
holdings.statement: Reasonableness has become the default standard of review, especially when the decision-maker interprets its home statute.

holdings.quote: Ultimately, the difference between correctness and reasonableness comes down to deference. Deference is the attitude that must be adopted when conducting a reasonableness review. Deference means that on some questions, the reviewer must respect the decision-maker’s conclusions and accept them, even if the reviewer would have concluded differently based on the same arguments and evidence. This is because certain questions can be legitimately answered by an administrative decision‑maker in more than one way (Dunsmuir at para 47).
holdings.statement: Reasonableness review requires deference to the decision-maker's conclusions, accepting them even if the reviewer would have decided differently, because some questions can be legitimately answered in more than one way.

holdings.quote: A correctness standard, on the other hand, requires no deference – the decision lies with the reviewer and no margin for error exists for the decision‑maker below. The reviewer undertakes its own analysis of the question raised (Dunsmuir at para 50; British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal v Schrenk, 2017 SCC 62 at para 28).
holdings.statement: Correctness review requires no deference; the reviewer undertakes its own analysis and the decision-maker has no margin for error.

holdings.quote: It is clear that the first issue is reviewable on a reasonableness standard because it involves the interpretation of IRPA, the RAD’s home statute (Huruglica at para 30). This gives rise to a presumption of reasonableness, which has not been rebutted here (Williams Lake Indian Band v Canada (Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development), 2018 SCC 4 at para 138; Barreau du Québec v Quebec (Attorney General), 2017 SCC 56 at para 15).
holdings.statement: The first issue, interpretation of IRPA (the RAD's home statute), is reviewable on a reasonableness standard with a presumption of reasonableness that has not been rebutted.

holdings.quote: The second issue of whether the RAD’s Decision was reasonable in light of the answer to the first question is also reviewable on a reasonableness standard, since it involves a matter of mixed fact and law (Huruglica at para 35).
holdings.statement: The second issue, whether the RAD's decision was reasonable in light of the first, is also reviewable on a reasonableness standard as it involves mixed fact and law.

holdings.quote: When it comes to questions of home statute interpretation, the range of reasonable answers can still be very narrow (Huruglica at para 44). In fact, sometimes the ordinary tools of statutory interpretation will permit only one reasonable answer (McLean v British Columbia (Securities Commission), 2013 SCC 67 at para 38; Canada (Canadian Human Rights Commission) v Canada (Attorney General), 2011 SCC 53 at paras 34,64).
holdings.statement: Even under reasonableness review of home statute interpretation, the range of reasonable answers can be very narrow or even a single answer.

holdings.quote: Therefore, for the issues at bar, I must decide whether the RAD’s conclusions were reasonable — whether they were justified, transparent, and intelligible, and if they fall within the range of answers that are defensible in fact and law (Dunsmuir at para 47). Rather, the RAD’s conclusion and the process of how the tribunal reached that outcome must be justified, transparent and intelligible.
holdings.statement: The RAD's conclusions must be justified, transparent, intelligible, and fall within a defensible range in fact and law under reasonableness review.

holdings.quote: Although I am applying a reasonableness standard of review to these issues, and although the first issue may only have a very narrow range of reasonable answers or even a single answer, I must still be careful not to conduct a disguised correctness review. That would be to decide, in my view, the bull’s eye answer and then find that any other answer is unreasonable.
holdings.statement: Applying reasonableness review requires avoiding disguised correctness review by not deciding the single 'bull's eye' answer and rejecting all others as unreasonable.

holdings.quote: To undertake this analysis, I will divide the first issue into the following three questions: (i) Did the RAD reasonably conclude that it must apply two standards of review — correctness to most of the RPD’s findings, and deference to some of the RPD’s findings relating to credibility? (ii) Did the RAD reasonably identify the conditions triggering the deferential standard? (iii) Did the RAD reasonably define the content of the deferential standard?
holdings.statement: The court divides the first issue into three questions about the RAD's conclusions on its standard of review: whether the RAD reasonably concluded it must apply two standards of review, whether it reasonably identified the conditions triggering the deferential standard, and whether it reasonably defined the content of the deferential standard.

holdings.quote: Specifically, when the RPD makes a credibility finding based on oral evidence, and that finding is then challenged by way of appeal to the RAD, how does the RAD go about determining whether it should intervene? That is really what is meant by standard of review.
holdings.statement: The standard of review question is how the RAD determines whether to intervene on RPD credibility findings based on oral evidence when appealed to the RAD.

holdings.quote: Under a correctness standard, the RAD intervenes if the finding does not line up with its own reading of the record. If deference is due, then another framework must guide the RAD’s review for error.
holdings.statement: Under a correctness standard, the RAD intervenes if the finding does not align with its own reading of the record; if deference is due, a different framework guides the RAD's review for error.

holdings.quote: While the statutory interpretation proposed by CARL/CCR may have some merit, this Court is nonetheless constrained by the case law to conduct a reasonableness review of the RAD’s Decision, particularly in light of the Federal Court of Appeal’s observations in Huruglica. In my view, to construe the Federal Court of Appeal’s comments as being strictly limited to deference on remedy, as CARL/CCR assert, would strain the text of that judgment given how the concept of deference is ordinarily understood.
holdings.statement: The Court is constrained by case law to conduct a reasonableness review of the RAD's decision, particularly in light of the Federal Court of Appeal's observations in Huruglica, and finds that construing Huruglica as limiting deference to remedy would strain the judgment's text.

holdings.quote: With respect to the Applicants’ position that deference can co-exist with a correctness review of all factual findings, I do not agree. Rather, correctness as a standard of review is defined by the absence of deference (Dunsmuir at para 34). In Maritime Broadcasting System Limited v Canadian Media Guild, 2014 FCA 59, the Federal Court of Appeal wrote: “[c]orrectness review has always been review without any deference. ‘Correctness with a degree of deference’ is a non-sequitur. It would be like describing a car as stationary but moving” (at para 60).
holdings.statement: The Court disagrees with the Applicants' position that deference can coexist with a correctness review of all factual findings, stating that correctness as a standard of review is defined by the absence of deference, citing Dunsmuir and Maritime Broadcasting System Limited v Canadian Media Guild.

holdings.quote: With this image in mind, the materials before me do not reflect that the Federal Court of Appeal envisioned a role for deference in the manner suggested by the Applicants. As a result, I am not persuaded by the Applicants’ argument that the RAD must apply a single correctness review to all of the RPD’s findings, and defer by showing restraint before applying correctness – even though I recognize that Huruglica at paragraph 70 (reproduced above) mentioned a degree of restraint twice.
holdings.statement: The Court finds that the Federal Court of Appeal did not envision a role for deference in the manner suggested by the Applicants, and is not persuaded that the RAD must apply a single correctness review to all RPD findings with deference shown as restraint before correctness.

holdings.quote: [W]here a serious issue of credibility is involved, fundamental justice requires that credibility be determined on the basis of an oral hearing.
holdings.statement: Where a serious issue of credibility is involved, fundamental justice requires that credibility be determined on the basis of an oral hearing.

holdings.quote: Appellate courts are well aware of the inherent weakness of written transcripts where questions of credibility are at stake and thus are extremely loath to review the findings of tribunals which have had the benefit of hearing the testimony of witnesses in person.
holdings.statement: Appellate courts are extremely loath to review findings of tribunals that have had the benefit of hearing witnesses in person due to the inherent weakness of written transcripts in credibility assessments.

holdings.quote: To the contrary, given the statutory analysis in Huruglica, this was clearly an outcome open to the RAD.
holdings.statement: Given the statutory analysis in Huruglica, the RAD's conclusion on applying two standards of review was clearly an outcome open to it.

holdings.quote: First, in judicial review, the standard of review flows from a contextual analysis, unless the jurisprudence has already determined which standard applies to a particular category of question (Dunsmuir at para 62).
holdings.statement: The standard of review flows from a contextual analysis unless jurisprudence has already determined the applicable standard for a category of question (Dunsmuir at para 62).

holdings.quote: Generally, deference is owed on questions of fact (see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 [Khosa] at para 89, Rothstein J, concurring).
holdings.statement: Generally, deference is owed on questions of fact (Khosa at para 89).

holdings.quote: When an appeal court reviews alleged errors of fact, a deferential standard of “palpable and overriding error” applies (Housen v Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33 [Housen] at para 10).
holdings.statement: When an appeal court reviews alleged errors of fact, a deferential standard of 'palpable and overriding error' applies (Housen at para 10).

holdings.quote: Broadly speaking, one reason to apply a deferential standard of review to findings of fact is that first instance decision‑makers are thought to be better-positioned to assess credibility, due to their expertise in making factual findings and their ability to see and hear witnesses (see Khosa at para 89; Housen at paras 12–14,18).
holdings.statement: One reason to apply a deferential standard of review to findings of fact is that first instance decision-makers are better positioned to assess credibility due to their expertise and ability to see and hear witnesses (Khosa at para 89; Housen at paras 12–14,18).

holdings.quote: The RAD, of course, is distinct from an appellate court, and thus many of the justifications for the deferential standard outlined in Housen (including respect for the integrity of the trial process and judicial economy) do not apply.
holdings.statement: The RAD is distinct from an appellate court, so many justifications for deferential standard outlined in Housen do not apply to the RAD, including respect for trial process integrity and judicial economy.

holdings.quote: In the Decision, the RAD majority decided, based on its reading of Huruglica, that a deferential standard was only appropriate where the RPD truly had a meaningful advantage in making the finding at issue. The RAD majority held that such a determination must be made on a case-by-case basis and, where the RAD concludes that a meaningful advantage existed, it must explain why.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority decided that a deferential standard is appropriate only where the RPD truly had a meaningful advantage in making the finding at issue, and such determination must be made case-by-case with explanation.

holdings.quote: In my view, the RAD majority’s conclusions on the conditions triggering a deferential standard of review are unreasonable. This is because the RAD majority failed to identify any principled framework for determining whether the RPD had a meaningful advantage in making a credibility finding in a given case.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority’s conclusions on the conditions triggering a deferential standard of review are unreasonable because they lack a principled framework for case-by-case determination of meaningful advantage.

holdings.quote: Although the RAD majority found that the RPD may be in a better position to make certain findings when it has seen, heard, and questioned a witness, it offered no way to determine if such a meaningful advantage truly exists on a case-by-case basis.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority failed to provide a method to determine if a meaningful advantage truly exists in each case.

holdings.quote: However, the RAD then provided little direction for identifying when such an advantage arises: for most of its categories, the RAD finds that meaningful advantage, if it existed, would arise as a result of the RPD seeing and hearing the claimant and witnesses.
holdings.statement: The RAD provided little direction for identifying when a meaningful advantage arises, often relying solely on the RPD seeing and hearing the claimant and witnesses.

holdings.quote: Although the RAD majority held that the RPD may have a meaningful advantage in situations where it has heard and seen a witness, in its subsequent review of the merits of the RPD’s decision it found that the RPD did in fact have a meaningful advantage whenever the finding at issue related to the Applicants’ oral testimony.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority found a meaningful advantage whenever the finding related to oral testimony without explaining why this always triggers deference.

holdings.quote: As noted by the Applicants, these conditions of seeing and hearing the witness will always be present at an RPD hearing.
holdings.statement: Seeing and hearing the witness will always be present at an RPD hearing and thus cannot alone justify deference.

holdings.quote: I note that the rationale of the RAD on these points has been found reasonable by this Court on judicial review, see, for instance, Odia v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 363 [Odia]:
holdings.statement: The rationale of the RAD on these points has been found reasonable by this Court on judicial review, for instance in Odia v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 363.

holdings.quote: Under the approach taken in these three RAD decisions and in Odia, a deferential standard of review is applied only where a correctness review would not be practicable.
holdings.statement: A deferential standard of review is applied only where a correctness review would not be practicable, as shown in the approach taken in the three RAD decisions and in Odia.

holdings.quote: This is consistent with Ozdemir v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 621, in which Justice Zinn held that it was unreasonable for the RAD to review the RPD’s credibility findings on a deferential standard, when the RAD was in as good a position as the RPD to assess the evidence:
holdings.statement: It was unreasonable for the RAD to review the RPD’s credibility findings on a deferential standard when the RAD was in as good a position as the RPD to assess the evidence, as held in Ozdemir v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 621.

holdings.quote: If meaningful advantage occurs only where the RPD bases its decision on some factor that cannot be reproduced in the record, the situations in which the RPD is truly meaningfully advantaged would be relatively rare (see also R v NS, 2012 SCC 72 [R v NS] at paras 98–102 (Abella J, dissenting)).
holdings.statement: If meaningful advantage occurs only where the RPD bases its decision on some factor that cannot be reproduced in the record, the situations in which the RPD is truly meaningfully advantaged would be relatively rare.

holdings.quote: I agree with the interveners that the record before the RAD should, in most cases, fully disclose the information on which the RPD based its findings and permit the RAD to review them on a correctness basis.
holdings.statement: The record before the RAD should, in most cases, fully disclose the information on which the RPD based its findings and permit the RAD to review them on a correctness basis.

holdings.quote: In my view, anything less would be inconsistent with the RPD’s duty to make its credibility findings in clear and unmistakeable terms (Hilo v Canada (Employment & Immigration), [1991] FCJ No 228 (Federal Court of Canada – Appeal Division) at para 6).
holdings.statement: Anything less would be inconsistent with the RPD’s duty to make its credibility findings in clear and unmistakeable terms, as stated in Hilo v Canada (Employment & Immigration), [1991] FCJ No 228 (Federal Court of Canada – Appeal Division) at para 6.

holdings.quote: Further, as a consequence of this duty, the RPD ends up creating a record that is commensurate with the RAD’s robust appellate role.
holdings.statement: As a consequence of this duty, the RPD ends up creating a record that is commensurate with the RAD’s robust appellate role.

holdings.quote: Of course, this also assumes that the RPD can, on occasion, reasonably make a credibility finding based on information to which the RAD would not have access on appeal.
holdings.statement: It is assumed that the RPD can, on occasion, reasonably make a credibility finding based on information to which the RAD would not have access on appeal.

holdings.quote: However, I have not been persuaded to depart from the views of higher courts as well as a long line of jurisprudence from my Federal Court colleagues, that seeing and hearing a witness may confer a fact-finding advantage to the RPD (see, for instance, Paye v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 685 at para 14 with respect to the RAD and Rahal v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 319 at paras 41–45). This type of thinking is reasonable and underpins deference to factual findings in other areas of law.
holdings.statement: Seeing and hearing a witness may confer a fact-finding advantage to the RPD, which is reasonable and underpins deference to factual findings in other areas of law.

holdings.quote: What was not reasonable for the RAD majority, however, was to give no guidance on how this factor should be considered under the categories they discuss.
holdings.statement: It was not reasonable for the RAD majority to give no guidance on how the factor of RPD's proximity to witness should be considered under the categories they discuss.

holdings.quote: Matters simply relating to oral testimony cannot suffice as a reason for deference. Rather, the relevant factors must relate to oral testimony and be incapable of being captured in the record before the RAD.
holdings.statement: Matters simply relating to oral testimony cannot suffice as a reason for deference; relevant factors must relate to oral testimony and be incapable of being captured in the record before the RAD.

holdings.quote: Only then could it be said that the RPD had a meaningful advantage over the RAD.
holdings.statement: Only when the RPD has a meaningful advantage over the RAD, based on factors not captured in the record, can deference be owed to the RPD.

holdings.quote: Instead of explaining this divide, and analyzing when having heard oral testimony confers a meaningful advantage, the RAD majority seems to reason that having heard oral testimony in and of itself confers a meaningful advantage. In the end, this begs the question of when the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage, because that tribunal always hears oral testimony.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority erred by reasoning that having heard oral testimony in and of itself confers a meaningful advantage, which begs the question of when the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage.

holdings.quote: In other words, the RPD always has a general advantage. The key question is, therefore, when that advantage becomes particular or specific to the oral testimony. Only then would it become a meaningful advantage, such that deference to the RPD is owed.
holdings.statement: The RPD always has a general advantage by hearing oral testimony; the key question is when that advantage becomes particular or specific to the oral testimony, thus becoming a meaningful advantage warranting deference.

holdings.quote: In my view, the divergence in subsequent RAD cases on this question, as pointed out above, is reflective of the deficiencies in the RAD majority’s model that make its Decision unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority's model is deficient and its decision unreasonable due to divergence in subsequent RAD cases on the question of deference.

holdings.quote: While I agree that these are both forms of deference, broadly construed, they do not assist in the real issue that was before the RAD — namely, how the RAD is supposed to tell if a specific credibility finding made by the RPD can stand.
holdings.statement: While institutional and remedial deference are forms of deference, they do not assist in determining how the RAD should assess if a specific RPD credibility finding can stand.

holdings.quote: I agree with CARL/CCR that, if an independent assessment is understood as equating to correctness, the RAD majority could not reasonably marry this concept with deference.
holdings.statement: If an independent assessment is understood as equating to correctness, the RAD majority could not reasonably marry this concept with deference.

holdings.quote: But this Court has also held that even a deferential review by the RAD involves an independent assessment of the evidence (see Guo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 317 at paras 15–19; Jeyaseelan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 278 at paras 19–21).
holdings.statement: Even a deferential review by the RAD involves an independent assessment of the evidence.

holdings.quote: What I take from the above case law is that, for most of the RPD’s findings, the RAD is required to conduct a correctness review and substitute its own conclusions where they differ from those of the RPD.
holdings.statement: For most of the RPD's findings, the RAD is required to conduct a correctness review and substitute its own conclusions where they differ from those of the RPD.

holdings.quote: But even for those findings that attract a deferential review, an independent assessment of some form is also needed. Deference never equates to blind endorsement (see Dunsmuir at para 48).
holdings.statement: Even for findings attracting deferential review, an independent assessment of some form is needed; deference does not equate to blind endorsement.

holdings.quote: In brief, after considering the RAD majority’s rationale, I do not find that their RAD reasonableness standard is distinguishable from the reasonableness standard used on judicial review merely because it necessitates an independent assessment.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority's reasonableness standard is not distinguishable from the judicial review reasonableness standard merely because it necessitates an independent assessment.

holdings.quote: I think it is obvious here that, regardless of the label it chose, the content of the deferential standard adopted by the RAD majority is duplicative of the framework to be applied on judicial review.
holdings.statement: The content of the deferential standard adopted by the RAD majority duplicates the framework applied on judicial review, regardless of the label used.

holdings.quote: In my view, the RAD majority’s conclusions on the content of its deferential standard are not consistent with the Federal Court of Appeal’s instructions that the RAD is not to review RPD decisions in the manner of a judicial review (Huruglica at paras 37, 47–48).
holdings.statement: The RAD majority’s conclusions on its deferential standard are inconsistent with the Federal Court of Appeal’s instructions that the RAD is not to review RPD decisions as a judicial review.

holdings.quote: Nonetheless, I find that the RAD majority’s explanation of RAD reasonableness only duplicates the task of a court on judicial review and, therefore, falls outside of the range of outcomes reasonably available to it.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority’s explanation of RAD reasonableness duplicates the task of a court on judicial review and falls outside the range of outcomes reasonably available to it.

holdings.quote: It is not my role to set out what the content of the RAD’s deferential standard should be. However, I observe that the RAD may have greater success in developing a RAD‑specific standard of deferential review if it first clearly identifies the conditions triggering deference — namely, what it means, in a concrete sense, for the RPD to have had a meaningful advantage in making a particular credibility finding.
holdings.statement: It is not the Court's role to set the content of the RAD’s deferential standard, but the RAD may succeed by clearly identifying conditions triggering deference, such as what it means for the RPD to have a meaningful advantage in credibility findings.

holdings.quote: More importantly, the content of the RAD’s deferential standard must be consistent with and animated by the purposes of its governing legislation (see Doshi v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FC 710 at paras 75, 80; see also Workers Comp of PEI v Dyment, 2016 PECA 10 at para 48).
holdings.statement: The content of the RAD’s deferential standard must be consistent with and animated by the purposes of its governing legislation.

holdings.quote: The RAD majority’s concept of the RAD reasonableness standard is indistinct from that of Dunsmuir in judicial review, and thus of incompatible with a full, fact based appeal.
holdings.statement: The RAD majority’s concept of reasonableness is indistinct from Dunsmuir judicial review and incompatible with a full, fact-based appeal.

holdings.quote: In my view, to be reasonable, a deferential standard selected by the RAD cannot simply duplicate the supervisory role of this Court on judicial review. The RAD reasonableness standard runs the risk of curtailing the opportunity to have flawed credibility determinations corrected.
holdings.statement: To be reasonable, a deferential standard selected by the RAD cannot simply duplicate the supervisory role of this Court on judicial review, as it risks curtailing correction of flawed credibility determinations.

holdings.quote: Given my conclusions on the first issue, it is neither appropriate nor necessary for me to comment on the RAD’s Decision insofar as it relates to the merits of the Applicants’ appeal.
holdings.statement: Given the conclusions on the first issue, it is neither appropriate nor necessary to comment on the RAD's Decision regarding the merits of the Applicants' appeal.

holdings.quote: The RAD’s Decision will accordingly be sent back to be decided anew by a differently constituted panel.
holdings.statement: The RAD's Decision will be sent back to be decided anew by a differently constituted panel.

holdings.quote: Having regard to the test for certification recently confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Lunyamila v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2018 FCA 22, I certify the following three questions: 1) Was it reasonable for the RAD to conclude that, under IRPA, some of the RPD’s findings are reviewable by it on a deferential (i.e. non-correctness) standard? 2) Was it reasonable for the RAD to conclude that the deferential standard applies where the RPD had a meaningful advantage in making the finding under review, and, if so, did the RAD articulate a reasonable framework for identifying such an advantage? 3) Was it reasonable for the RAD to adopt a deferential standard of RAD reasonableness, under which the RPD’s findings will be deferred to where the RAD can understand how they were reached, and where they were based on evidence in the record?
holdings.statement: I certify three questions for appeal regarding the reasonableness of the RAD's conclusions on standards of review and deferential standards.

holdings.quote: These three questions track the legal questions raised and are dispositive of these Reasons, in that they arise from the case itself rather than the way in which I disposed of the application.
holdings.statement: The three certified questions are dispositive of these Reasons and arise from the case itself rather than the disposition of the application.

holdings.quote: The three issues also raise issues of broad significance and general importance, transcending the interests of the parties (Lewis v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2017 FCA 130 at para 36).
holdings.statement: The three certified questions raise issues of broad significance and general importance, transcending the interests of the parties.

holdings.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed.
holdings.statement: The application for judicial review is allowed.

holdings.quote: Three questions are certified in accordance with these Reasons.
holdings.statement: Three questions are certified for appeal in accordance with these Reasons.

holdings.quote: I wish to thank all counsel for their excellent submissions, which were of great assistance to the Court.
holdings.statement: The Court thanks counsel for their excellent submissions which were of great assistance.

holdings.quote: Determining the degree of deference is a risky topic.
holdings.statement: Determining the degree of deference owed by the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) is a complex and risky topic.

holdings.quote: If I were to qualify the RAD’s standard of review when it examines the RPD’s credibility findings, I would say that it should not be a standard that limits its authority to intervene.
holdings.statement: The RAD's standard of review when examining the RPD's credibility findings should not be so limited as to restrict the RAD's authority to intervene.

holdings.quote: Despite the RPD’s advantageous position in some cases, the RAD’s approach involves taking a step back in order to better proceed with an independent and careful analysis of the evidence before it in an effort to determine whether the RPD committed an error warranting the RAD’s intervention.
holdings.statement: Although the RPD may have an advantageous position in some cases, the RAD must take a step back to independently and carefully analyze the evidence to determine if the RPD committed an error warranting intervention.

holdings.quote: In current decisions of the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal, it is indicated in which types of cases the RPD finds itself in an advantageous position in relation to the RAD and vice versa.
holdings.statement: The Federal Court and Federal Court of Appeal have indicated in which types of cases the RPD has an advantageous position relative to the RAD and vice versa.

holdings.quote: For example, the Federal Court states that the RAD is as equally well-placed as the RPD to determine plausibility.
holdings.statement: The Federal Court has found that the RAD is as equally well-placed as the RPD to determine plausibility.

holdings.quote: The Federal Court also finds that it is appropriate for the RAD to give deference to the RPD regarding the authenticity of a document when the RAD does not have the original documents.
holdings.statement: The Federal Court has found it appropriate for the RAD to give deference to the RPD regarding the authenticity of a document when the RAD does not have the original documents.

holdings.quote: That being said, I am also of the opinion that there is no need for me to further discuss situations that may present themselves before the RAD as I fear that talking in generalities or establishing categories could give rise to rigidity where the RAD is concerned.
holdings.statement: There is no need to further discuss general situations that may arise before the RAD as discussing generalities or establishing categories could lead to rigidity in the RAD's approach.

holdings.quote: In each case, the RAD ought to determine whether the RPD truly benefited from an advantageous position, and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final decision in respect of the refugee claim”.
holdings.statement: In each case, the RAD should determine whether the RPD truly benefited from an advantageous position and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final decision on the refugee claim.

rebuttals.quote: The RAD does not perform a de novo review but is constrained by the record before it and its appellate function (Huruglica at paras 79, 103). Rather, I agree with the Applicants that because it is not the RAD’s role to carry out a de novo consideration of the claim, the RAD is tethered to the RPD’s decision (see, for instance, Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness) v Gebrewold, 2018 FC 374 at para 25).
rebuttals.court_answer: The RAD does not perform a de novo review but is constrained by the record before it and its appellate function, and is tethered to the RPD’s decision.

authorities.quote: This view of a reasonableness review has been consistently reinforced by the Supreme Court in the decade since Dunsmuir (see for instance, Canada (Canadian Human Rights Commission) v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 SCC 31 [CHRC] at para 55, and Wilson v Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd, 2016 SCC 29 at paras 21–22).
authorities.authority: The Supreme Court has consistently reinforced the reasonableness standard since Dunsmuir.

authorities.quote: Indeed, Professor Daly observed as much in a recent commentary on the RAD majority’s Decision, writing that the RAD reasonableness test developed in the majority Decision is difficult to distinguish from the test set out by the Supreme Court in Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 and Agraira v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36 (see Paul Daly, “Effective Administrative Appeals (Again): Re X, 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB)” (16 July 2018), online (blog): Administrative Law Matters, www.administrativelawmatters.com).
authorities.authority: Professor Daly observed that the RAD reasonableness test is difficult to distinguish from the Supreme Court's judicial review test in Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union and Agraira cases.

authorities.quote: I disagree. The Federal Court of Appeal, after reviewing the purposes of the governing legislation, held at paragraph 66 of Huruglica that the RAD is a sui generis statutory body whose role is to act as a safety net.
authorities.authority: The Federal Court of Appeal held in Huruglica that the RAD is a sui generis statutory body acting as a safety net, implying a different standard than Dunsmuir.

authorities.quote: Huruglica later referenced Minister Kenney’s promise of a “full, fact-based appeal” (Huruglica at para 94).
authorities.authority: Huruglica referenced Minister Kenney’s promise of a 'full, fact-based appeal'.

authorities.quote: As Justice Gauthier states, the degree of deference owed to the RPD “ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.
authorities.authority: Justice Gauthier's statement that the degree of deference owed to the RPD ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis is endorsed.

left_open.quote: Turning back to our dartboard, in a reasonableness review, as long as the decision‑maker hits a point that is not out of bounds, the reviewer will not intervene: s/he does not have to hit what the Court views as the bull’s-eye (Skinner at para 23). Accordingly, tribunal decisions do not have to be perfect. On review, they should be approached as an organic whole, rather than the reviewer conducting a line-by-line treasure hunt for errors (Communications, Energy and Paperworkers Union of Canada, Local 30 v Irving Pulp & Paper, Ltd, 2013 SCC 34 at para 54).
left_open.issue: In reasonableness review, the decision-maker need not hit the 'bull's-eye' but must not be 'out of bounds'; decisions are reviewed as a whole, not line-by-line for errors.
